members.local_label: Section 2.1 — null training sample, test sample and model
members.source_heading: Section 2.1 — null training sample, test sample and model
members.statement_original: As in Section 1.1, we let $Y = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$ denote the null training sample (NTS) with a common marginal distribution $P_0$, $X = (X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ the test sample with $X_i\sim P_i$ ($1\leq i\leq m$), $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_{n+m}) =(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n, X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ the full sample, ${\mathcal{H}}_0=\{1\leq i\leq m\::\: P_i = P_0\}$ the set of nulls in the test sample with $m_0 = |{\mathcal{H}}_0|, \pi_0 = m_0 / m$, and ${\mathcal{H}}_1=\{1,\dots,m\}\setminus {\mathcal{H}}_0$ the set of novelties with $m_1 = |{\mathcal{H}}_1|, \pi_1 = m_1 / m$. For notational convenience, we write $n+{\mathcal{H}}_0$ for the set $\{n+i,i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0\}$. Furthermore, we denote by $P$ the joint distribution of $Z$, which belongs to a family of distributions $\mathcal{P}$ (model).

members.local_label: Section 2.2 — false discovery rate and false discovery proportion, equation (2)
members.source_heading: Section 2.2 — false discovery rate and false discovery proportion, equation (2)
members.statement_original:
Given a procedure $R$, the false discovery rate (FDR) is defined as the expectation of the false discovery proportion (FDP) with respect to the distribution $P\in \mathcal{P}$: 
\[
\mathrm{FDR}(P,R)= \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P}[\mathrm{FDP}(P,R)],\:\:\: \mathrm{FDP}(P,R)=\frac{\sum_{i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0} {\mathbb{1}\left\{i\in R\right\}}}{1\vee |R|}.\tag{2}
\]

members.statement_original:
Suppose a set of $p$-values $(p_i,1\leq i\leq m)$ is available, the BH algorithm Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) returns $R = \{i\in \{1,\dots,m\}\::\:p_i\leq \alpha \hat{k}/m\},$ where $\alpha$ is the target FDR level and 
\[
\hat{k} = \max\left\{k\in \{0,\dots,m\}\::\: \sum_{i=1}^m {\mathbb{1}\left\{p_i\leq \alpha k/m\right\}}\geq k\right\}.\tag{4}
\]

members.statement_original:
In this paper, we propose a method called AdaDetect. It is an adaptive novelty detection procedure that extends the existing strategies described in Weinstein et al. (2017), Yang et al. (2021), Mary and Roquain (2022), and Bates et al. (2021). It starts by splitting the null sample $(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)$ in two samples $(Y_1,\dots,Y_k)$ and $(Y_{k+1},\dots,Y_{n})$ with $k\geq 0$. To avoid cluttering our notation, we define $\ell$ as the size of the second null sample, i.e., $\ell=n - k.$ It proceeds with the following steps.

1.  Compute a data-driven score function of form 
\[
g(z)=g(z,(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k}), (Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n +m})),\:\:\: z\in \mathcal{Z},\tag{7}
\]
 which satisfies the following invariance property: for any permutation $\pi$ of $\{k+1,\dots,n+m\}$ and $z,z_1,\dots,z_{n+m}\in \mathcal{Z}$, we have 
\[
g(z,(z_{1},\dots,z_{k}), (z_{\pi(k+1)},\dots,z_{\pi(n +m)}))=g(z,(z_{1},\dots,z_{k}), (z_{k+1},\dots,z_{n +m})).\tag{8}
\]


2.  Transform the raw data into univariate scores 
\[
S_i = g(Z_i; (Z_1,\dots,Z_k) , (Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n+m})), \quad i \in \{ k+1, \ldots,n+m\}.\tag{9}
\]
 Here, we assume that novelties typically have large scores.

3.  For each test point $X_j$, generate the empirical $p$-value by comparing $S_i$ with the scores in the NTS: 
\[
p_j = \frac{1}{\ell+1}\left(1+\sum_{i=k+1}^{n}{\mathbb{1}\left\{S_i>S_{n+j}\right\}}\right), \:\:j\in\{1,\dots,m\}.\tag{10}
\]


4.  Apply the BH algorithm to $(p_1,\dots,p_m)$ at the target level $\alpha$.

We will call this procedure $\mbox{AdaDetect}_\alpha$ in the sequel to emphasize the target level.

members.statement_original: $(S_{k+1}, \ldots, S_{n+m})$ have no ties almost surely.

Following Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001), we say a family of $p$-values $(p_i,1\leq i\leq m)$ is PRDS on ${\mathcal{H}}_0$ if, for any $i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0$ and nondecreasing[^1] measurable set $D\subset [0,1]^m$, the function $u\in [0,1]\mapsto \mathbb{P}((p_j,1\leq j\leq m)\in D\:|\: p_i= u)$ is nondecreasing.

[^1]: A set $D\subset [0,1]^m$ is said to be nondecreasing if for any $x\in D$ and $y\in [0,1]^m$, we have $y\in D$ provided that $y_i\geq x_i$ for all $i$.

members.local_label: Section 4.1 — average densities and gamma, equations (15)-(17)
members.source_heading: Section 4.1 — average densities and gamma, equations (15)-(17)
members.statement_original:
Let 
\[
f=\pi_0 f_0+ \pi_1 \bar f_1,\tag{15}
\]



\[
\bar f_1= m_1^{-1}\sum_{i\in {\mathcal{H}}_1} f_i.\tag{16}
\]
 Under Assumptions 4 and 5, $f_0$ is the average density of $(Z_1,\dots,Z_k)$, $\bar{f}_1$ is the average alternative density, $f$ is the average density of the test sample $(X_1,\dots,X_m)$. Similarly the average density of $(Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n+m})$ is $f_\gamma$ where


\[
\gamma=\frac{m_1}{\ell+m};\:\:\:\:\:\:
f_\gamma=(1-\gamma) f_0 + \gamma \bar{f}_1 =\frac{\ell}{\ell+m} f_0+ \frac{m}{\ell+m} f.\tag{17}
\]

evidence.location: Section 4.1 — average densities and gamma, equations (15)-(17)

members.statement_original:
Lastly, we define the density ratio 
\[
r(x)= \frac{\pi_1 \bar f_1(x)}{ f(x)}, \quad x\in \mathcal{Z}.\tag{18}
\]
 Note that $r(x)\in (0,1)$ for $\nu$-almost every $x\in \mathcal{Z}$ by Assumption 5.

Recall that AdaDetect is equivalent to applying the counting knockoff on the scores which relies on an estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}$ (Section 2.4). For each given $t$, when $\ell$ and $m$ is large, $\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}(t)\approx m \:\mathbb{P}_{S_i\sim P_0}(S_i \ge t)/\mathbb{E}[|R(t)|] \approx \mathbb{E}[|R(t)\cap \{k+1, \ldots, n\}|]/\mathbb{E}[|R(t)|],$ where $R(t)$ is set of rejections at threshold $t$. The RHS is called the marginal FDR (mFDR), an error metric that is close to FDR when $|R(t)|$ is large and often used for asymptotic power analysis of FDR-controlling procedures e.g. Sun and Cai (2007); Lei and Fithian (2018). The following theorem derives the optimal score function among all procedures that reject hypotheses with $S_i$ above some thresholds subject to mFDR control (see Weinstein (2021); Rosset et al. (2022) for results for FDR instead of mFDR).
members.variant_note: The printed ratio intersects R(t) with calibration indices, although Section 2.2 defines rejection sets using test indices. This indexing ambiguity and the displayed approximations are preserved.

members.statement_original: The oracle AdaDetect procedure, denoted by AdaDetect$^*$, is defined as the AdaDetect procedure with the score function $r(\cdot)$ defined in (18).

Since AdaDetect is invariant under any strictly monotone transformation of the score function (see Remark 2.1), AdaDetect$^*$ can be realized as any AdaDetect procedure with a score function of the form 
\[
g^*= \Psi \circ r, \mbox{ for some increasing continuous $\Psi:(0,1)\to {\mathbb{R}}$},\tag{19}
\]
 where $\Psi$ could depend on unknown parameters. This is a crucial property of AdaDetect that enables flexible classification methods to construct score functions without concerning about the composition of nulls and novelties that may change the oracle score $r$.
